blocks.content: 1. Introduction

A distributed system is a collection of independent machines that communicate over a network to appear as a single coherent service. The moment you split a program across more than one machine, you inherit a new category of problems that a single process never has to think about. A function call that used to be a guaranteed, near instant operation becomes a network request that can be slow, can be dropped, can time out, or can succeed on the server while the confirmation never makes it back to the caller.

This lesson is about that shift in thinking. It covers why failure has to be treated as the normal case rather than the exception, the different shapes failure can take, the standard toolkit engineers use to keep systems working when parts of them break, and how to reason through all of this out loud in a system design interview.
In a single process, a call either returns or the whole program crashes. In a distributed system, a call can fail in ways that leave you unsure whether anything happened at all.
2. Why Failure Is the Default Assumption
blocks.text: 2. Why Failure Is the Default Assumption

blocks.content: New engineers often design distributed systems as if the network were a reliable wire connecting two functions. Experienced engineers design as if the network is actively hostile, because over a long enough time horizon, at large enough scale, it behaves that way. A service that talks to ten downstream dependencies, each with 99.9 percent availability, is mathematically limited to well under 99 percent availability of its own unless it actively compensates for those dependencies failing.

The numbers get worse quickly at scale. A fleet of ten thousand servers, each with an average uptime of ninety nine point nine percent in a given year, will statistically have around ten machines down at any given moment purely from that baseline failure rate, before counting deployments, kernel upgrades, or hardware faults. A system designed for a world where nothing goes wrong will spend its entire life in a state its designers never planned for.
2.1 The Fallacies of Distributed Computing

In the 1990s, engineers at Sun Microsystems, including L Peter Deutsch, catalogued a set of assumptions that programmers repeatedly and wrongly make when writing networked software. These became known as the fallacies of distributed computing, and every one of them still shows up in production incidents today.

["The network is reliable: packets are dropped, connections reset, and routers fail more often than most designs admit.","Latency is zero: a call across a data center, let alone across regions, always costs real milliseconds that add up.","Bandwidth is infinite: shared links saturate under load and become a bottleneck nobody planned for.","The network is secure: every hop is a potential point of interception or tampering unless explicitly protected.","Topology does not change: nodes are added, removed, and rescheduled constantly in modern cloud environments.","There is one administrator: large systems span teams and organizations with no single point of control.","Transport cost is zero: serialization, connection setup, and encryption all consume real CPU and time.","The network is homogeneous: real traffic crosses a mix of hardware, protocols, and providers with different behavior."]
items: The network is reliable: packets are dropped, connections reset, and routers fail more often than most designs admit.
Latency is zero: a call across a data center, let alone across regions, always costs real milliseconds that add up.
Bandwidth is infinite: shared links saturate under load and become a bottleneck nobody planned for.
The network is secure: every hop is a potential point of interception or tampering unless explicitly protected.
Topology does not change: nodes are added, removed, and rescheduled constantly in modern cloud environments.
There is one administrator: large systems span teams and organizations with no single point of control.
Transport cost is zero: serialization, connection setup, and encryption all consume real CPU and time.
The network is homogeneous: real traffic crosses a mix of hardware, protocols, and providers with different behavior.

blocks.title: Why This List Still Matters
blocks.content: None of these fallacies are exotic edge cases. Every large scale outage postmortem you will ever read traces back to a team having quietly assumed one of these eight statements was true.

Once you accept that the network is unreliable, slow sometimes, and outside your full control, the entire discipline of failure handling stops looking like defensive extra work and starts looking like the actual job of building a distributed system.
3. Categories of Failure

Not all failures look alike, and the difference matters because each category needs a different detection strategy and a different fix. Broadly, failures in a distributed system fall into four buckets: crash failures, network partitions, slow or degraded nodes, and byzantine failures.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286530090-359785023.png
blocks.alt: Four categories of failure branching from a single root: crash failure, network partition, slow or degraded node, and byzantine failure

blocks.content: 3.1 Crash Failures

A crash failure is the simplest and most forgiving kind: a process stops entirely and stays stopped. It does not respond, it does not send partial or corrupted data, it just goes silent. This is sometimes called a fail stop failure, and it is the easiest failure mode to design around because the behavior is unambiguous once detected.
3.2 Network Partitions

A network partition happens when a subset of nodes can no longer communicate with another subset, even though every individual node is still alive and healthy. From inside one partition, the nodes on the other side look exactly like they have crashed, which is precisely what makes partitions dangerous: a perfectly healthy node can be mistakenly declared dead, and a system can end up with two halves both believing they are in charge.

This is the scenario the CAP theorem describes: when a partition occurs, a system must choose between staying available and answering with data that might be stale, or staying strictly consistent and refusing to answer at all until the partition heals.
3.3 Slow or Degraded Nodes

This is the category that causes the most production pain in practice, precisely because it is the hardest to detect. A node that is up, reachable, and passing its health check, but responding ten times slower than usual, does not trip any of the alarms a crashed node trips. Callers keep sending it work, threads pile up waiting on it, and the slowdown spreads outward.
3.4 Gray Failures

Engineers sometimes call this specific pattern a gray failure, as opposed to the black and white clarity of a full crash. A disk that is failing but not yet dead, a garbage collection pause that stretches every few minutes, or a network interface silently dropping a percentage of packets, all produce this kind of degraded, half working state that monitoring built only to detect total outages will miss entirely.
3.5 Byzantine Failures

A byzantine failure is the most severe and least common category: a node keeps responding, but its responses are wrong, inconsistent, or actively malicious rather than simply absent or slow. The name comes from the Byzantine Generals Problem, a thought experiment about reaching agreement when some participants may be lying. Most application backends never have to defend against genuinely byzantine behavior, because they control every server in their own data center. Systems that do need to defend against it include blockchain networks, multi party financial settlement systems, and anything accepting input from hardware or clients you do not fully trust.

4. Failure Detection vs Failure Recovery

It helps to keep two questions completely separate when designing for failure. The first question is detection: how does the system find out that something has gone wrong. The second question is recovery: once it knows, what does it actually do about it. Conflating these two leads to designs where a system technically notices a problem but has no defined action to take, or takes action based on a signal that was never reliable in the first place.
4.1 Failure Detection

Detection usually relies on one of a small set of signals. Heartbeats are periodic pings a node sends to say it is still alive, and the absence of a heartbeat past some threshold is treated as a failure signal. Health checks are active probes, typically an HTTP endpoint, that a load balancer or orchestrator calls to decide whether a node should keep receiving traffic. Timeouts detect failure indirectly, by treating the absence of a response within an expected window as evidence that something is wrong, even without a direct signal.

More advanced systems use adaptive detectors, such as a phi accrual failure detector, which does not use a single fixed timeout but instead builds a statistical model of normal response timing and flags a node as suspect once its behavior deviates enough from that baseline. This reduces both false positives during normal jitter and slow detection during genuine outages.
4.2 Failure Recovery

Recovery is the set of actions triggered once a failure is detected. This can mean failing over to a replica, restarting a crashed process, retrying a request against a different instance, rerouting traffic away from an unhealthy zone, or in the worst case falling back to a degraded mode of operation while a human is paged. Recovery strategies need to be designed in advance. Discovering a failure with no predefined recovery path just turns an outage into a longer outage while someone improvises.
4.3 Observability as the Foundation of Detection
blocks.text: 4.3 Observability as the Foundation of Detection

blocks.content: None of the detection signals above are useful without visibility into what a system is actually doing. Structured logs, request level tracing across service boundaries, and metrics on latency, error rate, and saturation are what let an on call engineer tell the difference between a genuine crash, a slow dependency, and a client sending malformed requests. Teams that invest in observability find failures in minutes. Teams that do not, find them from customer complaints.

blocks.title: Percentiles Over Averages
blocks.content: Average latency hides the problem you actually care about. A service can have a perfectly healthy average response time while its ninety ninth percentile is ten times worse, meaning one in a hundred users is having a bad experience right now. Failure detection dashboards should track p50, p95, and p99 separately, not just the mean.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396524930-663510240.png
blocks.alt: An order placement flow checking whether a circuit breaker to the payment service is open, charging the card or queuing the order as pending payment

blocks.title: The Timeout Tradeoff
blocks.content: Set your detection timeout too short and healthy but momentarily slow nodes get falsely marked as dead, causing needless failovers. Set it too long and a genuinely dead node keeps receiving traffic for longer than necessary. There is no universally correct number, only a tradeoff tuned to how costly each type of mistake is for your specific system.
5. Key Resilience Techniques

Once you accept that dependencies will fail, a standard toolkit exists for containing the damage. None of these techniques prevent failure. All of them limit how far a failure spreads and how badly it affects the parts of the system that are still healthy.
5.1 Retries With Backoff and Jitter

A retry simply means trying the same operation again after it fails, on the assumption that many failures are transient, a brief network blip, a momentarily overloaded server, a load balancer routing to an instance mid restart. Retrying blindly and immediately is dangerous: if a downstream service is struggling under load, an immediate retry from every failed caller adds more load at the exact moment the service can least handle it.

Exponential backoff fixes this by waiting longer between each successive attempt, typically doubling the wait time, so retry traffic backs off as failures continue. Jitter adds a small random amount to that wait time so that many clients who failed at the same instant do not all retry at the exact same instant again, which would otherwise recreate the very overload the backoff was meant to avoid.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286533901-156647956.png
blocks.alt: Four retry attempts against a failing call, with wait time roughly doubling with added jitter until the fourth attempt succeeds

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Recovers automatically from transient blips without any human intervention","A struggling downstream service can be pushed into full collapse by a wave of retries, sometimes called a retry storm"],["Smooths out brief spikes in error rate that would otherwise surface as user facing failures","Retries can multiply latency, a request that should fail fast in 50 milliseconds instead takes several seconds across attempts"],["Cheap to implement and works for most idempotent read style operations","Retrying a non idempotent operation can duplicate the effect of that operation if not handled carefully"]]}
5.2 Retry Storms

A retry storm happens when a large number of clients all start retrying against the same struggling dependency at roughly the same time, and the combined retry traffic is larger than the original load that caused the slowdown in the first place. This is how a minor blip turns into a full outage. A dependency running at ninety percent capacity that starts failing ten percent of requests can be pushed to well over one hundred percent of its capacity the moment every one of those failed calls is retried on top of ongoing new traffic.

blocks.title: Guarding Against Retry Storms
blocks.content: Cap the total number of retries in flight system wide, not just per request, and consider a retry budget that stops issuing new retries once a percentage of overall traffic is already retries. Combining backoff with jitter and a circuit breaker is what actually prevents a storm, backoff alone is not enough when thousands of clients fail in the same second.
5.3 Timeouts

A timeout is a hard limit on how long a caller will wait for a response before giving up and treating the call as failed. Without a timeout, a single slow dependency can hold a thread, a connection, or a resource indefinitely, and enough of those held resources will exhaust the caller entirely. Every network call in a distributed system should have an explicit timeout. Relying on the operating system or library default is a common source of outages, because those defaults are frequently far longer than any acceptable user facing wait time.
5.4 Circuit Breakers

A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and tracks the recent failure rate. While failures stay below a threshold, the breaker is closed and calls pass through normally. Once failures cross that threshold, the breaker trips open, and for a cooldown period every call fails immediately without even attempting the network request. This protects the caller from wasting time and resources on a dependency that is clearly already in trouble, and it protects the struggling dependency from being hit with continued load while it tries to recover.

After the cooldown period, the breaker moves to a half open state and allows a small number of trial calls through. If those succeed, the breaker closes again and normal traffic resumes. If they fail, the breaker reopens and the cooldown restarts.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396524932-817639827.png
blocks.alt: A circuit breaker moving from closed to open once a failure threshold is crossed, to half open where a trial call decides whether to close or reopen

blocks.content: 5.5 Redundancy and Replication

Redundancy means running more than one copy of a critical component so that the failure of any single instance does not take down the whole service. Replication is the data specific version of this idea, keeping copies of the same data on multiple nodes so a read or write can succeed even if one replica is unreachable. The tradeoff is consistency: keeping replicas in perfect agreement at all times costs latency, so most systems choose a consistency model, strong, eventual, or something in between, that matches what the data actually needs.

["Leader follower replication: one node accepts writes and streams them to followers, giving a clear source of truth at the cost of a single write bottleneck and a failover step when the leader dies.","Multi leader replication: more than one node accepts writes, improving write availability across regions at the cost of having to resolve conflicting writes to the same record.","Quorum based replication: a write or read only needs to succeed against a majority of replicas, allowing the system to tolerate a minority of nodes being down without pausing entirely."]
items: Leader follower replication: one node accepts writes and streams them to followers, giving a clear source of truth at the cost of a single write bottleneck and a failover step when the leader dies.
Multi leader replication: more than one node accepts writes, improving write availability across regions at the cost of having to resolve conflicting writes to the same record.
Quorum based replication: a write or read only needs to succeed against a majority of replicas, allowing the system to tolerate a minority of nodes being down without pausing entirely.

blocks.content: 5.6 Graceful Degradation

Graceful degradation means a system keeps serving its core function even when a non critical dependency is unavailable, by temporarily reducing functionality rather than failing entirely. This requires deciding in advance which features are essential and which can be sacrificed under stress.

blocks.title: Graceful Degradation in Practice
blocks.text: An e-commerce product page normally shows a personalized recommendation carousel powered by a recommendation service. If that service times out, a well designed page falls back to a static list of best sellers, or simply hides the carousel, and still renders the product details, price, and buy button without delay. A poorly designed page instead lets the whole request hang waiting on recommendations, turning a minor, non critical outage into a total inability to buy anything.

blocks.content: 5.7 Bulkheading

Bulkheading takes its name from the watertight compartments in a ship, where flooding in one compartment is contained instead of sinking the entire vessel. Applied to software, it means isolating resources, thread pools, connection pools, or entire service instances, per dependency, so that one dependency being slow cannot exhaust resources needed to serve calls to a completely different, healthy dependency.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286539811-524669043.png
blocks.alt: A shared thread pool exhausted by a slow recommendation service, which then also stalls the unrelated search and cart services

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286541453-586908021.png
blocks.alt: The same three services with isolated thread pools per dependency, so the recommendation service times out alone while search and cart continue normally

blocks.content: 5.8 Load Shedding

Load shedding means deliberately rejecting some incoming requests so the system can keep serving the rest, rather than accepting every request and degrading so badly that it can serve none of them well. A server that queues every request indefinitely under overload eventually falls over entirely. A server that rejects the newest requests once its queue passes a safe depth keeps latency bounded for everyone it does serve.

A common pattern is to shed low priority traffic first, background jobs and non essential analytics calls, while continuing to serve requests tied directly to revenue or safety. This requires classifying request priority ahead of time, since deciding what to drop in the middle of an incident is too slow and too error prone.
6. Idempotency and Safe Retries

Every retry strategy quietly depends on one assumption: that performing the same operation more than once has the same effect as performing it exactly once. Without that guarantee, retries stop being a safety mechanism and start being a new source of bugs, duplicate charges, duplicate emails, duplicate orders.
6.1 What Idempotency Means
An operation is idempotent if calling it once and calling it many times with the same input produces the same end result.

Reading a value is naturally idempotent, reading it ten times does not change anything. Setting a field to a specific value is idempotent, setting it to the same value repeatedly leaves the same end state. Incrementing a counter is not idempotent by default, calling increment three times instead of once due to a retried request leaves the counter at a different value than intended. The same is true of anything that appends, charges, or sends, unless it is explicitly designed to detect and ignore duplicates.
6.2 Techniques for Making Retries Safe

["Idempotency keys: the client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it with every attempt, including retries, so the server can recognize and discard duplicates.","Deduplication tables: the server records which idempotency keys it has already processed and the result it returned, replaying that stored result instead of redoing the work on a repeated request.","Conditional writes: a write includes a precondition, such as an expected current version, so a duplicate write either has no effect or is rejected outright if the state has already moved on.","Designing operations to be naturally idempotent where possible, such as expressing a payment as set balance to this exact value rather than subtract this amount from balance."]
items: Idempotency keys: the client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it with every attempt, including retries, so the server can recognize and discard duplicates.
Deduplication tables: the server records which idempotency keys it has already processed and the result it returned, replaying that stored result instead of redoing the work on a repeated request.
Conditional writes: a write includes a precondition, such as an expected current version, so a duplicate write either has no effect or is rejected outright if the state has already moved on.
Designing operations to be naturally idempotent where possible, such as expressing a payment as set balance to this exact value rather than subtract this amount from balance.

blocks.title: A Common Mistake
blocks.content: Generating a new idempotency key on every retry attempt defeats the entire purpose. The key must represent the logical operation, the same key on attempt one, attempt two, and attempt three, so the server can recognize them as the same request.
7. Worked Example: Order Processing During a Payment Outage
blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: Order Processing During a Payment Outage

blocks.content: Consider an order processing system for an online store. A customer places an order, the order service validates the cart, reserves inventory, then calls an external payment service to charge the card, and finally confirms the order. Now suppose the payment service, entirely outside this team's control, starts timing out for fifteen minutes during a provider side incident.
7.1 What Goes Wrong Without Protection

If the order service calls the payment provider with no timeout, requests pile up holding open connections and threads until the whole order service runs out of capacity, and customers cannot even browse the catalog, let alone check out. If it retries immediately and aggressively without backoff, it adds load onto a payment provider that is already struggling, potentially delaying that provider's own recovery. If a retry duplicates a charge because the request was not idempotent, some customers get billed twice for a single order, which is a far worse outcome for trust than a slow checkout.
7.2 Designing the Order Service to Handle This
blocks.text: 7.2 Designing the Order Service to Handle This

blocks.content: ["Set an explicit, short timeout on the call to the payment provider, so a single slow request cannot hold resources indefinitely.","Wrap the payment call in a circuit breaker, so once failures cross a threshold, further calls fail fast instead of waiting on a service that is clearly down.","Attach an idempotency key derived from the order id to every payment attempt, so retries never risk a duplicate charge.","When the breaker is open, do not fail the order outright. Instead, place it in a pending payment state and enqueue it for asynchronous retry once the provider recovers.","Show the customer an honest, specific status, your order is confirmed and payment is processing, rather than either a hard failure or a false success.","Run a reconciliation job afterward that checks every pending order against the payment provider's actual records, to catch any edge cases the retry logic missed."]
items: Set an explicit, short timeout on the call to the payment provider, so a single slow request cannot hold resources indefinitely.
Wrap the payment call in a circuit breaker, so once failures cross a threshold, further calls fail fast instead of waiting on a service that is clearly down.
Attach an idempotency key derived from the order id to every payment attempt, so retries never risk a duplicate charge.
When the breaker is open, do not fail the order outright. Instead, place it in a pending payment state and enqueue it for asynchronous retry once the provider recovers.
Show the customer an honest, specific status, your order is confirmed and payment is processing, rather than either a hard failure or a false success.
Run a reconciliation job afterward that checks every pending order against the payment provider's actual records, to catch any edge cases the retry logic missed.

blocks.title: Walking Through One Request
blocks.text: A customer places order 8841 at the exact moment the payment provider begins failing. The first call times out after three seconds. The circuit breaker, seeing several recent failures across other orders, is already open, so the order service does not even attempt the call again immediately. It marks order 8841 as pending payment and returns a success response to the customer confirming the order was received. A background worker retries the payment call every thirty seconds using the same idempotency key, order dash 8841 dash charge dash one. Twelve minutes later the provider recovers, the retry succeeds exactly once, and the order moves to confirmed. The customer never saw an error, and the card was charged exactly once.

blocks.content: This example ties every technique in this lesson together. Timeouts stop one slow call from spreading damage. The circuit breaker stops the order service from hammering an already failing provider. Idempotency makes retrying safe rather than risky. Graceful degradation, showing pending instead of failed, keeps the customer experience intact. And detection versus recovery are handled as two separate concerns, the breaker detects the outage, the background job and reconciliation handle recovering from it.
8. Discussing Failure Handling in a System Design Interview
blocks.text: 8. Discussing Failure Handling in a System Design Interview

blocks.content: Interviewers bring up failure handling because it separates candidates who can describe a happy path architecture from candidates who have actually operated systems in production. Bringing it up yourself, unprompted, at the right point in the interview is one of the strongest signals you can give.
8.1 What Interviewers Are Listening For

["Whether you treat failure as an afterthought or as a first class part of the design, brought up naturally rather than only when pressed.","Whether you can name the specific failure mode you are protecting against, rather than gesturing vaguely at making the system reliable.","Whether you understand the tradeoff each technique introduces, not just its benefit, such as retries risking overload or strong consistency risking availability during a partition.","Whether you can reason about a concrete scenario, such as what happens if this specific downstream dependency goes down for ten minutes, rather than staying abstract."]
items: Whether you treat failure as an afterthought or as a first class part of the design, brought up naturally rather than only when pressed.
Whether you can name the specific failure mode you are protecting against, rather than gesturing vaguely at making the system reliable.
Whether you understand the tradeoff each technique introduces, not just its benefit, such as retries risking overload or strong consistency risking availability during a partition.
Whether you can reason about a concrete scenario, such as what happens if this specific downstream dependency goes down for ten minutes, rather than staying abstract.

blocks.content: 8.2 A Simple Framework to Structure Your Answer
blocks.text: 8.2 A Simple Framework to Structure Your Answer

blocks.content: ["Identify the dependency that can fail and describe what its failure would look like from the caller's perspective, slow, error, or silently wrong.","State how you would detect that failure, a timeout, a health check, an elevated error rate.","State how you would contain it, a circuit breaker, a bulkhead, load shedding, so the failure does not spread to unrelated parts of the system.","State how you would recover, retry with backoff if idempotent, failover to a replica, or degrade gracefully if the dependency is non essential.","Mention the tradeoff explicitly, for example that a fallback to cached data means occasionally serving slightly stale results in exchange for staying available."]
items: Identify the dependency that can fail and describe what its failure would look like from the caller's perspective, slow, error, or silently wrong.
State how you would detect that failure, a timeout, a health check, an elevated error rate.
State how you would contain it, a circuit breaker, a bulkhead, load shedding, so the failure does not spread to unrelated parts of the system.
State how you would recover, retry with backoff if idempotent, failover to a replica, or degrade gracefully if the dependency is non essential.
Mention the tradeoff explicitly, for example that a fallback to cached data means occasionally serving slightly stale results in exchange for staying available.

blocks.title: Interview Tip
blocks.content: When asked how you would handle a downstream dependency going down, resist the urge to jump straight to just retry it. A strong answer walks through detection, containment, and recovery as three distinct steps, and names the specific tradeoff each choice introduces.
9. Summary

Distributed systems fail constantly, in different shapes, for different reasons, and the fallacies of distributed computing explain why assuming otherwise leads to fragile designs. Crash failures are the easiest to handle because they are unambiguous. Network partitions and slow or degraded nodes are harder because a struggling node can look identical to a healthy one from the outside. Byzantine failures matter mainly in adversarial or safety critical contexts.

["Detection and recovery are separate concerns, and a design needs an explicit answer for both.","Timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, redundancy, graceful degradation, and bulkheading form the standard toolkit for containing failure.","Idempotency is what makes retrying safe in the first place, without it retries trade one problem for a worse one.","The worked order processing example shows these techniques working together rather than in isolation, which is exactly how they show up in real systems.","In an interview, naming the specific failure mode, its detection signal, its containment strategy, and its tradeoff is far stronger than a general claim that a system will be reliable."]
items: Detection and recovery are separate concerns, and a design needs an explicit answer for both.
Timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, redundancy, graceful degradation, and bulkheading form the standard toolkit for containing failure.
Idempotency is what makes retrying safe in the first place, without it retries trade one problem for a worse one.
The worked order processing example shows these techniques working together rather than in isolation, which is exactly how they show up in real systems.
In an interview, naming the specific failure mode, its detection signal, its containment strategy, and its tradeoff is far stronger than a general claim that a system will be reliable.

blocks.content: A system that has never been designed to fail well will eventually fail badly. The only choice you actually have is whether that failure is contained or catastrophic.
